answer:
**Natural-language hypothesis (final deliverable)**

In the NLSY79 1989 cross-section (N = 10,535 after removing 2,151 exact-row duplicates), respondent AGE in 1989 has no statistically reliable cross-sectional association with the probability of withdrawing more from savings than depositing (DISSAVED = 1) once log income, gender, and race indicators are controlled. In the primary controlled model (M3: logit P(DISSAVED=1) = AGE + AGE^2 + log(INCOME+1) + GENDER_MALE + BLACK + HISPANIC), the age coefficients are small and statistically non-significant — β_AGE = +0.220 (SE 0.250, z = 0.88, p = 0.380) and β_AGE^2 = −0.0038 (SE 0.0045, z = −0.85, p = 0.396) — and a likelihood-ratio test of M2 versus M1 fails to reject the linear form (χ²(1) = 0.746, p = 0.388). The model is therefore consistent with a near-linear (effectively flat) age profile of net withdrawal, not with a robust quadratic hump. Direct numerical evidence: the M3 fitted curve across ages 24–32 moves only from 0.268 → 0.285 → 0.276 (peak at age 29), and the binned empirical DISSAVED rates span 0.262–0.302 with overlapping 95% CIs; the average marginal effect of one additional year of AGE on P(DISSAVED = 1) is +0.044 (SE 0.050, n.s. at conventional levels) — that is, at most about 4 percentage points per decade of age, statistically indistinguishable from zero. Direction of the point estimate is mildly positive, not negative. A life-cycle hump cannot be ruled out — the implied logit-polynomial turning point sits at age 28.7, inside the observed band — but because AGE and AGE^2 are highly collinear across this 8-year window and β_AGE^2 is not credibly identified, no concave-withdrawal-with-age pattern is supported. A sensitivity refit of M3 on the un-deduplicated full sample (N = 12,686) does return a marginally significant inverted-U (β_AGE^2 = −0.0088, p = 0.043; β_AGE = +0.443, p = 0.067), showing that the duplicates had been inflating an apparent age pattern; the substantive null on the deduplicated sample is therefore the conservative conclusion. Functionally, in this 24–32 NLSY79 window the only strong, statistically significant drivers of DISSAVED are log income (β = +0.250, p < 10⁻²⁴), Black race (β = +0.176, p < 0.001), and male gender (β = −0.128, p = 0.003); Hispanic ethnicity is null (p = 0.79). **Bottom line:** once income, gender, and race are held constant, age in this 24–32 late-twenties window exerts at most a small, statistically indistinguishable effect on the likelihood of withdrawing more from savings than depositing, and the data are consistent with effectively no (or a near-linear, negligible) age association rather than a quadratic hump.

payload.hypothesis: In the deduplicated NLSY79 1989 cross-section (N = 10,535), AGE in 1989 has no statistically reliable cross-sectional association with the probability of withdrawing more from savings than depositing once income, gender, and race are controlled (M3: β_AGE = +0.220 [p = 0.380]; β_AGE^2 = −0.0038 [p = 0.396]; LR M2 vs M1: χ²(1) = 0.746, p = 0.388; AME of AGE on P(DISSAVED=1) = +0.044 per year, SE 0.050, n.s.). The data are consistent with a near-linear (effectively flat) age profile, not with a robust quadratic hump, across the observed 24–32 window in which AGE and AGE^2 are highly collinear.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 rows) and verified all 9 documented columns + zero missingness + AGE_2 == AGE**2. 2) Dropped 2,151 exact-row duplicates for the primary sample (N_dedupe = 10,535). 3) Fit three nested logistic regressions via statsmodels.Logit on the deduplicated sample: M1 (DISSAVED ~ AGE), M2 (M1 + AGE_2), and M3 (M2 + log(INCOME+1) + GENDER_MALE + BLACK + HISPANIC). 4) Likelihood-ratio test M1 vs M2 returned chi2 = 0.746, p = 0.388 (no curvature support). 5) Computed implied logit turning point age* = -beta_AGE/(2*beta_AGE2) = 28.72 (in-band) but conditional on imprecisely estimated beta_AGE2. 6) Computed the overall AME of AGE on the probability scale using statsmodels DiscreteMargins (dy/dx = +0.044, SE = 0.050) plus a manual finite-difference cross-check. 7) Generated an SVG plus ASCII fallback plot of P(DISSAVED=1) versus AGE at M3 sample-mean controls with the binned empirical rates overlaid (95% CIs). 8) Refit M3 on the full un-deduplicated N = 12,686 sample as a sensitivity check (beta_AGE2 = -0.0088, p = 0.043, indicating duplicates were inflating an apparent age effect). 9) Serialised all coefficients, SEs, z, p, 95% CIs, log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, McFadden R^2, LR test, AME, turning point, fitted curve, and per-bin rates to artifacts/results.json.
